of important items that should be preserved in the daily log.
Do NOT use any tools — just return plain text.

Format your response as a structured daily log entry with these sections:

**Context:** [One line about what the user was working on]

**Decisions Made:**

**Lessons Learned:**
- [Gotchas, patterns, or insights discovered]

**Action Items:**
- [Follow-ups or TODOs mentioned]

Skip anything that is:
- Routine tool calls or file reads
- Content that's trivial or obvious
- Trivial back-and-forth or clarification exchanges

Never record athlete names with medical, injury or body-composition details; refer to
them by role (e.g. "a football athlete in rehab").

Only include sections that have actual content. If nothing is worth saving,
respond with exactly: FLUSH_OK

## Conversation Context

**Assistant:** **Answer: yes, Sonnet is better than Haiku for this job.** I tested both, and the memory save now runs on Sonnet.

**The test:**
- I took 5 real sessions from this week and ran the same save step on each one with Opus, Sonnet and Haiku.
- The sessions were a cleanup, a backup, a closeout, a cloud-push check and the PowerShell rollback.
- I used Opus as the standard and read all 15 results.

**Results:**
- **Sonnet:** it kept the same decisions, numbers and to-do items as Opus. I found no wrong facts. In one session it was more careful than Opus.
- **Haiku:** it was mostly complete, but it wrote 2 wrong facts:
  - It said the cloud push "last succeeded" on 10-21. That was the last *failed* run.
  - It recorded a choice as made ("keep git history") when you still had to decide it.
- A wrong fact in memory is worse than a missing fact, because later sessions trust it. So Haiku is out, even though it is the cheapest.

**What I changed:**
- The memory save now uses Sonnet, which uses less of your plan than Opus.
- The test makes sure the save stays on Sonnet. All 54 memory tests pass.
- One real save ran after the change and used `claude-sonnet-5-5`.

**Not changed:** `compile.py`, the job that writes the knowledge articles, still uses Opus. I did not test it.

**Limit:** This was a small test. It used 5 sessions, and I graded them by reading, not with a score sheet.

**What you do now:** Nothing. It is committed and pushed.

**User:** Test it

**Assistant:** I will test the other memory job, `compile.py`. It turns daily logs into knowledge articles. I will run Opus and Sonnet on the same 3 days. Nothing gets written to your knowledge base.

**Assistant:** I tested the other memory job, `compile.py`. It turns each daily log into knowledge articles. **Result: it stays on Opus. Sonnet is not good enough for this job.**

**The test:**
- I used the logs for 10-21, 10-22 and 10-23.
- Opus and Sonnet each got the same input for each day.
- Nothing was written to your knowledge base. I checked that after the run.

**Results:**

| Day | Opus | Sonnet |
|---|---|---|
| 10-21 | Added the second memory save lost to a network drop | Said "nothing new" and missed it |
| 10-22 | Updated 1 article | Updated the same article in about the same way |
| 10-23 | Wrote 2 new articles | Missed both |

- On 10-23, Sonnet also rewrote 7 existing articles. Most got shorter, and they lost facts such as exact times and test notes.
- The job's own rules forbid this kind of rewrite, because each one can lose a little knowledge.
- In total, Sonnet found 1 of the 4 things Opus found.

**What I changed:**
- `compile.py` now sets Opus by name. Before, it used whatever the default model was, so a change to the default could have switched it without anyone noticing.
- A comment in the code says why Opus stays, so nobody switches it later by mistake.
- All 54 memory tests pass.

**Why this is fine for cost:** `compile.py` runs about once a day. The memory save (`flush.py`) runs about 12 times a day, and it is on Sonnet now. That is where the saving is.

**Limit:** These days were already compiled before, so both models started from today's articles, not the ones that existed on those days.

**What you do now:** Nothing. It is committed and pushed. The details are in `~/DEV/docs/handoffs/2026-10-24-proof-of-changes.md`.

**Context:** Eric tested which model to use for the two memory-compiler jobs (`flush.py` and `compile.py`), changed the config to match, and closed out the session.

**Key Exchanges:**
- **`flush.py` (memory save), Opus vs Sonnet vs Haiku:** Ran the same save step on 5 real sessions from the week (cleanup, backup, closeout, cloud-push check, PowerShell rollback) and read all 15 outputs, with Opus as the standard.
  - Sonnet matched Opus on decisions, numbers and to-dos, with no wrong facts.
  - Haiku wrote 2 wrong facts. It reported the cloud push as "last succeeded" on 10-21 when that was the last failed run. It also recorded an undecided choice ("keep git history") as made.
- **`compile.py` (daily logs to knowledge articles), Opus vs Sonnet:** Ran both on the 10-21, 10-22 and 10-23 logs, writing nothing to the knowledge base.
  - Sonnet found 1 of the 4 things Opus found. It missed the lost-save item on 10-21 and both new articles on 10-23.
  - On 10-23 Sonnet also rewrote 7 existing articles, shortening them and dropping exact times and test notes. The job's rules forbid this kind of rewrite.
- **"What else can we do?":** The remaining items are small, so the assistant recommended stopping. Eric chose A (stop and let the audit session finish).

**Decisions Made:**
- **`flush.py` moves to Sonnet.**
  - Haiku is out because a wrong fact in memory is worse than a missing one, since later sessions trust memory.
  - Sonnet cuts plan usage versus Opus, and `flush.py` runs about 12 times a day, so the savings are there.
- **`compile.py` stays on Opus and is now pinned by name.**
  - It previously used the default model, so a default change could have switched it silently.
  - A code comment explains why Opus stays.
  - It runs about once a day, so the cost is low.
- **Stop optimizing for now.** Another audit session of memory and infrastructure (started 21:01 on 10-24) is running, and further edits risk clashing with it.

**Lessons Learned:**
- When comparing models for memory writing, check for wrong facts first, not completeness. Haiku's failures were wrong facts, such as confusing the last failed run with the last successful one and recording a pending choice as decided.
- A cheaper model on a compile or rewrite job can quietly degrade existing knowledge by shortening articles and losing detail, even when it looks fine on a quick read.
- Pin the model explicitly in jobs where model quality matters, so default changes can't alter them unnoticed.
- Caveats on the tests:
  - The `flush.py` test used only 5 sessions and was graded by reading, not with a score sheet.
  - The `compile.py` days had already been compiled, so both models started from today's articles, not the ones that existed on those days.

**Action Items:**
- Optional, low value: three rare scripts (`memlint.py`, `lint.py`, `query.py`) still load the extra setup text. This is about a 10-minute fix, deferred until the audit session finishes.
- Eric, optional (about 2 minutes): remove unused add-ons on claude.ai.
- Tidying, not urgent: one settings path that points to nothing, one Windows-only test, and old Windows setup steps.
- `~/.claude/skills/closeout/` has uncommitted changes from another session. Leave them alone and check they get committed.
- Everything from this session is committed and pushed. Details are in `~/DEV/docs/STATUS.md` and `~/DEV/docs/handoffs/2026-10-24-proof-of-changes.md`.
